newsitem.title: UK: N.Ireland talks mired as arms plan faces defeat.
newsitem.headline: N.Ireland talks mired as arms plan faces defeat.

text.p: Anglo-Irish proposals that Northern Ireland guerrillas disarm while pursuing peace talks faced defeat on Wednesday, casting a cloud over over plans to forge an end to decades of conflict.

Britain's Northern Ireland Secretary, Mo Mowlam, said she expected the "parallel decommissioning" proposal to be voted down when parties to the talks are balloted on 50-odd amendments to the plan on Wednesday.
"It's not a disaster, it is clearly a setback but no one ever said this would be easy," Mowlam told reporters a few hours before particpants in the multi-part talks began voting in mid-afternoon.

Defeat would leave unresolved the single most contentious issue in a peace process started in December 1993, and throw into doubt plans to begin substantive negotiations on a lasting settlement by the two governments' target date of September 15.
Hardline pro-British loyalist leader Ian Paisley said the vote would spell the end of the talks, which his Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) has already said it is leaving after the Wednesday vote.
"... all the to-ing and fro-ing of the Secretary of State (Mowlam) between this and September cannot resurrect these talks," he told reporters.
Mowlam said that, even if the proposals were voted down, the two governments would maintain their target date of September 15 to begin talks on a settlement.

But political sources said failure to agree how and when guerrillas could disarm might torpedo chances of getting the unionists and Sinn Fein, political wing of Irish Republican Army (IRA) guerrillas, to the same negotiating table.
Sinn Fein chairman Michel Mclaughlin accused unionists of holding the talks to ransom over decommissioning.

"People are attempting to apply a veto on the political process and the peace process and it is not acceptable. It will spell for all of us a return to the conflict and the division that we were hopefully about to leave behind us," he said.
David Trimble, leader of the most powerful Protestant group, the Ulster Unionist Party, said he would probably vote against the proposals but would not leave the negotiations.
Trimble wants the talks underpinned by a decommissioning plan that would commit Sinn Fein and its Protestant loyalist extremist foes to handing over weapons during the talks.

The British and Irish governments reply that the proposals, framed as a compromise after more than a year of stalemate, say guerrillas should disarm during the talks. Trimble wants the wording of any plan to change that "should" to "must".

He and fellow unionist parties, two of which have said they are walking out of the negotiations after Wednesday's vote, believe that last weekend's ceasefire by the IRA is just a ruse to get Sinn Fein admitted to the talks in September.
Britain says Sinn Fein, which seeks to end British rule of Northern Ireland, can join the talks when they begin their substantive work in September providing the IRA truce is real.
But Trimble said the IRA might abandon its truce, as it did a previous ceasefire called in August 1994, if the talks do not lead to the end of British rule.
"It's very easy to turn off violence for a couple of weeks. The important thing is what do they intend. The worry is that this ceasefire is just as cynical as the last one," he said.
Saturday's IRA ceasefire declaration pledged an unequivocal restoration of the previous, broken truce but made no mention of any end to the war against British rule.
The arms proposals apply to all political groups with guerrilla allies including loyalist extremists already represented at the negotiations since an October 1994 ceasefire.

The proposals back "parallel decommissioning" as a way of breaking deadlock between unionists, who say the IRA must disarm before Sinn Fein can take its place at the talks, and Sinn Fein's stance that disarmament should be part of a final settlement.
The IRA sees itself as an anti-colonial guerrilla army and says it will not hand over a single bullet until a final settlement is reached.

Decommissioning has divided the key protagonists for almost four years since Britain and Ireland unveiled their "Downing Street Declaration", which promised a seat at peace talks to any group which repudiated violence.
